doc.title: Anne Phillips interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 24, 2025

title: Studio camaraderie: Sammy Davis Jr., Joe Wilder, Artie Butler
summary: Anecdotes of friendship among session players, including Sammy Davis Jr. and Claus Ogerman.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: But the wonderful thing was that everybody was such good friends. I mean I remember doing a big thing and we finished a take, I think it was one of the Pepsi things. And it was a big thing. And whoever was in the booth said, “I’ll buy that.” And from the back of the

percussion section George Devin said, “I’m not selling.” And I’ll tell you one of the great things, I mean there was so much friend and camaraderie on it. I was doing a session, I contracted the voices for — oh come on, come on, okay I’ll get it in a minute, but nevertheless the voices were in the booth and in the connecting booth was the artist who was Sammy Davis Junior. And this was Claus Ogerman, there we are. And Claus had his hands up in the air and I’m in the booth with my hands up ready to cue the singers when Sammy leans out of his booth and grabs my arm and he says, “You see all those little brown spots? Did it ever occur to you that if they got together you’d be colored?” Claus heard, “not a beautiful ooo.”
That’s terrific. Did you ever work with Joe Wilder?
Oh what a delightful person he was.
Yes, absolutely. See those were the people that were around and playing record dates, all those greatest.

It’s funny, Dick Hyman made a comment at the time playing some of those pop tunes and they would joke about, “Just think, in twenty years people were saying, ‘they’re playing our song.’” And he says and they were. That’s what happened.
Yes. It was funny, Artie Butler — do you know Artie?
Artie some years ago said, “You know, remember how dumb we used to think some of those songs were? Today they sound like Mozart.”
